title: A binomial tree in C++
objectives: Port the Python binomial pricer to C++.
Price on one vector of n + 1 values, overwritten in place at each step back.

screens.title: One step back, in place
screens.prose:
Now one step back. At time $i$ there are $i + 1$ nodes, so only cells 0 to $i$ change:

$$v_j \leftarrow \text{disc}\,\big(q\,v_{j+1} + (1 - q)\,v_j\big).$$

Cells above $i$ keep stale values. Here is the two-step call from trees level 2, with $q = 0.625$ and disc $= 1/1.05$.
screens.question: Write `step_back`. It changes `v` in place and returns nothing.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each test runs your function on a small vector, then compares the whole vector within a relative 1e-9. Stale cells must be left alone.

hints.text: Which cells are rewritten, and which old values does each need?
The vector is passed by reference, so writing `v[j]` changes the caller's vector.
`for (int j = 0; j <= i; ++j) v[j] = disc * (q * v[j + 1] + (1 - q) * v[j]);`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 steps [1, 2, 4, 8] back once. If `v[1]` came out 4, your loop ran downwards and read a value it had just overwritten. Run `j` upwards.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `v[2]` still 44. Rewrite only cells 0 to `i`; the vector keeps its size.

explain.text: Running `j` upwards, `v[j]` is read before it is rewritten, and `v[j + 1]` is still old. Downwards, `v[j + 1]` would already hold the new value. The vector keeps its size; `i` says which cells matter.

screens.title: The whole pricer
screens.prose: Join the pieces. `tree_price` takes `growth`, what £1 grows to in one step. That is $1 + r$ on trees level 2's example, $e^{r\Delta t}$ on a calibrated tree. For an American option, compare with exercising at each node, spot $Su^jd^{i-j}$. `binomial_price` sets $\Delta t = t/n$, $u$ = `crr_u(sigma, dt)`, $d = 1/u$.
screens.question: Write `tree_price` and `binomial_price`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 11 hidden tests. Prices are accepted within a relative 1e-9; the 512-step call within 0.005 of 10.45. Two tests pass only if the program stops (throw `std::invalid_argument`): this browser build cannot catch exceptions.

hints.text: Order: check q, fill the leaves, then loop `i` from `n - 1` down to 0.
After `step_back(v, i, q, 1.0 / growth)`, an American option loops `j` from 0 to `i` once more.

`v[j] = std::max(v[j], payoff(s * std::pow(u, j) * std::pow(d, i - j)));` In `binomial_price`: `if (t == 0.0) return payoff(s);` then `tree_price(payoff, s, u, 1.0 / u, std::exp(r * dt), n, american)`.

feedback.correct: The Python pricer, in C++, to the same digits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is the American put, £7.99 with growth 1.05 per step. Take `std::max(hold, exercise)` at every node, with spot `s * std::pow(u, j) * std::pow(d, i - j)`.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 has t = 0: no time left, so return `payoff(s)` before dividing by n.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has σ = 0, so u = d = 1 and q divides by zero. Throw when q is not strictly between 0 and 1.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 grows £1 by 1.25 per step, above u = 1.2: an arbitrage, and q = 1.125. Refuse it.

explain.text: The two-step tests use growth $1 + r = 1.05$, as trees level 2 did; `binomial_price` uses $e^{r\Delta t}$, as trees l8 did. σ = 0 has no tree: q would divide by zero. A tiny σ such as 0.01, with enough steps, gives £4.88, the discounted forward payoff $e^{-rT}\max(Se^{rT} - K, 0)$.

screens.prose: Your `binomial_price` printed these calls. Inputs: $S = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $T = 1$, growth $e^{r\Delta t}$. Trees l8's Python gave the same numbers to about 15 significant figures. Black-Scholes, the limit, is £10.4506.

Below 10.4506 the error is negative.

feedback.correct: The error shrinks about four times for four times the steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each error is the C++ price minus 10.4506, with its sign.

explain.text: From 128 to 512 steps the error falls from −0.0156 to −0.0039, a quarter: it shrinks roughly like $1/n$. Odd and even n zigzag around the limit (trees l9), so compare like with like. C++ and Python agree because they do the same arithmetic in the same doubles.

screens.title: Days to expiry
screens.prose: A colleague prices a six-month at-the-money call with your pricer. His driver reads the days to expiry as an `int`.
screens.question: It prints 0. Why?

options.text: `days / 365` divides two `int`s, so `t` is 0 and the pricer returns the payoff
200 steps are too few
options.why: 200 steps leave an error of pennies, not £6.88. The price is exactly 0.

options.text: A `double` cannot hold 182/365
options.why: A `double` holds 0.4986 easily. The division happened in `int` arithmetic before the value reached `t`.

options.text: An at-the-money call is worth £0
options.why: Only at expiry. With half a year left this call is worth about £6.88.

hints.text: What are the types of `days` and `365`?
Line 2 divides first, then stores the result in a `double`.
`182 / 365` in `int` arithmetic is 0. With t = 0 the pricer returns `payoff(100)`, which is 0.

feedback.correct: Integer division threw away the whole half year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out `182 / 365` in C++.

byKey.double: A `double` holds 0.4986 easily. The division happened in `int` arithmetic before the value reached `t`.
byKey.atm: Only at expiry. With half a year left this call is worth about £6.88.

explain.text:
Python 3's `/` always gives a float; C++'s `/` on two `int`s drops the remainder. So `t` is 0, and the t = 0 branch returns the payoff at £100: £0. Make one side a `double`:

```cpp
double t = days / 365;     // int / int: 0
double t = days / 365.0;   // 0.4986
```

screens.title: Counting the work
screens.prose: The American branch recomputes each node's spot with two `std::pow` calls. Trees l9 counted the nodes of an $n$-step tree: $(n + 1)(n + 2)/2$.
screens.question: How many nodes does the 512-step American put visit?

hints.text: Put n = 512 into the formula.
The ten nodes here are $4 \times 5 / 2$, with n = 3.

feedback.correct: 131,841 nodes, so 263,682 `pow` calls for one price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $(n + 1)(n + 2)/2$ with n = 512.

byKey.row: 513 is one row, the memory we hold. The work visits every node of every row.
byKey.square: That is $512^2$, which counts a square grid. A recombining tree is a triangle, about half that.
byKey.n1n2: That is $512 \times 513 / 2$. Use $(n + 1)(n + 2)/2$: there are n + 1 rows, from 1 node to 513.

explain.text: Memory is one row of 513 doubles, but the work visits all 131,841 nodes. Two `pow` calls per node are correct and slow; level 3 times this and replaces them with a multiply. An `int` holds up to 2,147,483,647, so these counts and indices are safe.

explain.text: Reading into an `int` can fail, and then `n` holds garbage, so the check covers the read itself. `std::fixed` with `std::setprecision(4)` gives four places, like Python's `f"{price:.4f}"`. This is trees l8's pricer, rewritten in C++; level 3 times it.

ideas: A tree price needs one row at a time. Store the n + 1 leaf payoffs in a `std::vector<double>`. Overwrite cells 0 to i at each step back, counting j upwards.
`tree_price` takes the growth per step, so it reproduces both conventions. Those are $1 + r$ (trees level 2, £7.99 American put) and $e^{r\Delta t}$ (trees l8, £9.97 at n = 4).
C++ and Python agree to about 15 significant figures. The price converges like $1/n$ to £10.4506, zigzagging between odd and even n.

formula.note: $g$ is one step's growth: $1 + r$ or $e^{r\Delta t}$. American: then $v_j \leftarrow \max(v_j, f(Su^jd^{i-j}))$.

explain.text: Counting down, `v[i]` is rewritten first. Then the step for `j = i - 1` reads that new `v[i]` as if it were a later value. Counting up, each cell is read before it is rewritten.

It returns £4.88, the discounted forward payoff
options.why: That is the limit as σ falls, but the tree cannot reach it: with u = d, q is $(e^{r\Delta t} - 1)/0$.

options.why: With r = 5% the share still grows to £105.13, so the call is worth something. The tree just cannot represent it.
